Likewise
līk'wīz
adv. (in like manner, also; rendering Hebrew ken and gam, Greek homoios and hosautos)
A compound of like and wise (manner) — in like manner. It is the word by which a rule already stated is extended to a second case, and in the Gospels it repeatedly extends a warning or a judgment from one party to the hearer.

Biblical Definition

Likewise means in the same manner, and it is the hinge on which a stated principle is applied to a further case. The law uses it to extend a rule from one kind of firstling to another: “Likewise shalt thou do with thine oxen, and with thy sheep” (Exodus 22:30). Chronicles uses it of the Levites' duty morning and evening alike (1 Chronicles 23:30). But the Lord's uses are the arresting ones, because they turn a parable back on the hearer. He ends the parable of the unmerciful servant: “So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses” (Matthew 18:35) — the fictional king's severity applied without softening to the men listening. And twice in Luke 13, after news of Galileans killed by Pilate and of eighteen crushed by a tower, He refuses the question of comparative guilt and turns it on the crowd: “except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish” (Luke 13:5). The word denies every hearer the position of spectator.

Webster 1828 Definition

In like manner; also. It extends a stated rule to a further case, and in the Gospels it repeatedly turns a parable or a piece of news back on the hearer — so likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you.

expand to see more

LIKEWISE, adv. [like and wise, manner.] In like manner; also; moreover; too.

2. It extends to a second case what has been said of the first.

3. It answers to the Greek homoios and hosautos, in like manner.

4. It is used both to add a particular and to apply a principle.

5. In Scripture, So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, Matt. 18; except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish, Luke 13.

Key Scripture

Exodus 22:30 — "Likewise shalt thou do with thine oxen, and with thy sheep: seven days it shall be with his dam; on the eighth day thou shalt give it me."

Matthew 18:35 — "So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses."

Luke 13:5 — "I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish."

1 Chronicles 23:30 — "And to stand every morning to thank and praise the LORD, and likewise at even;"

Modern Corruption

Scripture is regularly read as though it were about other people. Likewise is the word that closes that escape: the parable's king, the tower at Siloam, the fate of the Galileans — each is turned on the man hearing.

expand to see more

Luke 13 shows the mechanism plainly. The crowd brings Christ a news item with a theological question attached: were these Galileans, whose blood Pilate mingled with their sacrifices, worse sinners than others? It is a comfortable question, because it invites a verdict on somebody else. He answers I tell you, Nay and adds the clause they did not ask for: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. Then, so that no one can attribute the first case to Roman politics, He supplies a second — the tower in Siloam, an accident with no villain — and repeats the sentence word for word.

The parable of the unmerciful servant closes the same way. A hearer may enjoy the story's justice from a distance, since the servant in it is plainly monstrous; then comes So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, with the qualification if ye from your hearts forgive not. James describes the alternative as a man beholding his natural face in a glass and going away and forgetting straightway what manner of man he was. The discipline the word enforces is simply to read every passage as addressed to oneself first, and to ask what must change here before asking who else needs to hear it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew extends with ken (so, thus) and gam (also); Greek uses homoios and hosautos, both meaning in like manner. The English compound joins like to wise, an old noun meaning manner.

expand to see more

Hebrew ken (H3651) — so, thus, in like manner; the ordinary particle of comparison.

Hebrew gam (H1571) — also, moreover; adds a further case to one already stated.

Greek homoios (G3668) — likewise, in like manner; the word in Luke 13:3 and 13:5.

Greek hosautos (G5615) — in the same way; used in the household codes of the epistles.

Saxon wise — manner, way; the noun surviving in likewise, otherwise, and nowise.

Usage

"Of a rule extended from one firstling to another: Likewise shalt thou do with thine oxen, and with thy sheep (Exodus 22:30)."

"Of a parable turned on the hearer: So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you (Matthew 18:35)."

"Of news refused as a verdict on others: except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish (Luke 13:5)."
